name: Jonas Lund, Open Call Club (2016)
why: Group show of 47 Rio de Janeiro artists selected from an open call by a bias-reversing algorithm; check whether the respondents' behaviour is the work.

name: Nadya Tolokonnikova, UnicornDAO (2022)
why: Artist-founded collector DAO for women, non-binary and LGBTQ+ artists; check whether its rules are an authored work.

name: UkraineDAO (2022)
why: Co-organised by Nadya Tolokonnikova; raised about $6.7M by auctioning an NFT of Ukraine's flag; collective purchase similar to AssangeDAO.

name: Solienne (Kristi Coronado with Eden, 2025)
why: AI artist agent shown in AUTOMATA at Paris Photo 2025; check its governance and collector rules.

name: Spirit Protocol (2025-26)
why: Announced 'social institution for synthetic beings' linked to Eden's autonomous AI artists; not yet public.

name: Eden (Gene Kogan and others)
why: Platform for autonomous generative AI agents; check which agents (Abraham, Solienne) have community-governed rules.

name: Zerebro (Jeffy Yu, 2024)
why: AI agent that posts, makes music and art, with a memecoin; compare with Truth Terminal.

name: Holly Herndon & Mat Dryhurst, Spawning / Have I Been Trained (2022)
why: Consent tools for AI training data; infrastructure rather than an artwork with a group protocol.

name: Caleb Larsen, A Tool To Deceive and Slaughter (2009)
why: Black box that keeps putting itself up for sale on eBay; precursor of self-selling artworks cited in the terra0 whitepaper.

name: Maria Eichhorn, Maria Eichhorn Aktiengesellschaft (2002)
why: Stock corporation at Documenta 11 whose shares could only be transferred to itself; cited by terra0 as a precursor of self-owning entities.

name: Wolfgang Müller, Knochengeld
why: Artist currency accepted in local bars and theatres that lost value every seven days; cited by terra0.

name: hitchBOT (David Harris Smith & Frauke Zeller, 2013-15)
why: Robot that could only travel if strangers picked it up; crossed Canada, Germany and the Netherlands; possible network/social entry.

name: Nouns-funded art (e.g. Nouns animation festival)
why: Nouns DAO has funded many art projects; include only those whose own rules shape collective behaviour.

name: Songcamp
why: Collaborative music collective running rule-based NFT music experiments (e.g. CHAOS, 2021); check authorship of rules.

name: Serpentine Arts Technologies / Legal Lab, Future Art Ecosystems
why: Research reports on DAOs and data trusts; theory rather than artworks.

name: Kevin Abosch, Forever Rose (2018)
why: Image token co-owned by ten collectors; check whether shared ownership rules shape behaviour (onchain batch).

name: Holly Herndon & Mat Dryhurst, Infinite Images and the Latent Camera (essay, 2022)
why: Essay on generative media and latent space that underpins Readyweights and xhairymutantx; possible theory entry, not about protocols or participation directly.

name: Strange Rules, Palazzo Diedo, Venice (4 May - 22 Nov 2026)
why: Protocol Art exhibition curated by Dryhurst, Herndon and Hans Ulrich Obrist with Adriana Rispoli (terra0, Primavera De Filippi, Ken Stanley, Citarella & New Models, Agnieszka Kurant and others); candidate exhibition collection, with a planned Protocol Art book.

name: Ken Stanley, Picbreeder (2007)
why: Online collective image-evolution site where users branch and evolve each other's images; shown in Strange Rules; check inclusion under network / collective-games.

name: Joshua Citarella & New Models, Marketplace of Ideas (2026)
why: New commission in Strange Rules; check whether it runs a participatory protocol.

name: Holly Herndon & Mat Dryhurst, Okayama Art Summit (2025)
why: Studio lists participation; work not identified.

name: Holly Herndon & Mat Dryhurst, MoMA x Feral File edition, Minnesang, I'M HERE 17122022 5:44 (2022-2023)
why: Editions and single works listed on the studio site with no documentation; not researched.

name: Stelarc — Fractal Flesh (1995)
why: Audiences in Paris, Helsinki and Amsterdam remotely actuated Stelarc's body via a web interface; a stronger crowd case than Ping Body.

name: Paul Ford — tilde.club (2014)
why: One unmodified Unix server where thousands made hand-coded homepages; an open-infrastructure case with a writer rather than artist as author.

name: Joel Holmberg — Legendary Account (2007–2010)
why: Earnest philosophical questions posted to Yahoo! Answers; the crowd's answers form the work.

name: Nick Thurston — Of the Subcontract (2013)
why: Book of poems written by Mechanical Turk workers, with their pay listed.

name: Blast Theory — Can You See Me Now? (2001)
why: Online players chased by runners in real streets; telematic game with a crowd of remote players.

name: Kit Galloway & Sherrie Rabinowitz — Electronic Café (1984)
why: Video and computer links between five Los Angeles community sites during the 1984 Olympic Arts Festival.

name: Alexei Shulgin — Desktop Is (1997)
why: Invited people to send screenshots of their desktops; early crowdsourced net-art exhibition.

name: Luther Blissett (1994)
why: Multiple-use name adopted by hundreds of activists and artists; open identity protocol, may fit autonomous-artists.

name: Rafael Lozano-Hemmer — Body Movies (2001) and other Relational Architecture works
why: Public-space works where crowds' shadows reveal portraits; check scope overlap with the social batch.

name: Lauren Lee McCarthy & Kyle McDonald — Noodle (2014)
why: A 'crowdsourced robot' whose actions are carried out by Mechanical Turk workers via a natural-language interface.

name: Reddit — Robin (2016), Sequence (2019), Second (2021)
why: Later Reddit April Fools' crowd experiments (vote to grow/stay/leave chats; crowd-sequenced film; guess the second most popular option); authorship not confirmed.

name: Aram Bartholl — DVD Dead Drop (2012) and OFFLINE ART (2013)
why: Read-only DVD burner in the Museum of the Moving Image wall, and an offline-router exhibition format; weaker crowd role than Dead Drops.

name: Kyle McDonald — Who Pays Artists? (2014)
why: Anonymous crowdsourced board where artists share what they were paid and by whom.

name: Harm van den Dorpel – Mutant Garden (web, c. 2019)
why: Visitors click a 'mutant' to replace its siblings with mutated offspring (single-parent breeding); a network-field candidate, not on-chain.

name: fxhash open-form generative art
why: fxhash format where each new edition can be minted from an existing one and inherits its lineage of hashes, so collectors grow a tree of variations; needs a specific artist's open-form project to qualify.

name: fxhash params (fx(params))
why: Collectors set artist-exposed parameters before minting; research specific works where collector choices shape the set.

name: Art Blocks PMP (project metadata parameters) projects
why: Art Blocks feature letting token owners configure artist-defined parameters after mint; find projects where owners' settings are the point.

name: Sam Spratt – Skulls of Luci / Council of Luci (2022)
why: 50 Skulls, 47 given as gifts to collectors, whose holders form the Council that judges later LUCI games; could be a separate governance entry.

name: Mathcastles – other works
why: Check Mathcastles' works beyond Terraforms (Xaltgeist and 0x113d) for further holder-driven systems.

name: Async Art – Blueprints and later programmable works
why: Other Async Art collaborations (e.g. layer works by XCOPY, Hackatao, Coldie) could be individual entries.

name: Words3 (on-chain word game)
why: Collaborative on-chain Scrabble-like board where players extend a shared grid; check authorship and whether it is an artwork.

name: Autonomous Worlds (ludens / 0xPARC essay, 2022)
why: Essay defining on-chain 'autonomous worlds' after Dark Forest; belongs in theory/crypto-theory.

name: Etheria (2015)
why: Early Ethereum hex-tile world where owners build on tiles; co-authored land precursor, likely provenance batch.

name: Pixelmap (Ken Erwin, 2016)
why: 3,970 tiles whose owners set their own pixel images on a shared map; early co-authored canvas, likely provenance batch.

name: Million Ether Homepage / Thousand Ether Homepage (2017)
why: Blockchain versions of the Million Dollar Homepage where buyers place pixels on a shared page.

name: Rare Pepe Directory (Counterparty, 2016)
why: Community-submitted card series admitted under published rules on Bitcoin/Counterparty; collective curation precursor.

name: Folia – Viper (Billy Rennekamp, 2022)
why: Snake-like NFT that grows as it is sent between people; ownership/transfer protocol, check with the ownership batch.

name: EulerBeats (2021)
why: Generative audio-visual originals whose prints follow a bonding curve and pay original holders; supply-mechanics candidate.

name: Bitcoin Ordinals recursive inscriptions
why: Look for artist-authored recursive-inscription projects where holders' inscriptions compose a shared work.

name: Higher (Farcaster, 2024)
why: Farcaster-born collective art movement around a shared word and token; check whether an authored rule set exists.

name: Fomo (Pak, 2021)
why: Free mint with fixed supply and a 50% secondary fee framed as partnership; check whether the fee rule shaped holder behaviour.

name: ASH Chapter II: Metamorphosis (Pak, March 2022)
why: Second ASH-only drop; mechanics not yet documented.

name: 404: The Presence of Absence (Pak)
why: Mentioned by collectors as a Pak project; date and rules unknown.

name: VV Editions: Humanity Check, 100 Meals (Jack Butcher, 2021)
why: Early 'infinite editions' by Visualize Value; check whether supply rules were a declared part of the work.

name: Hashmasks (Suum Cuique Labs, 2021)
why: 16,384 portraits whose names are set by holders by burning NCT tokens; collective naming as co-authorship.

name: Sam Spratt, The Monument Game (2023)
why: Holders of Spratt's works play a game that shapes the Luci narrative; possible co-authorship protocol.

name: Sarah Meyohas, Bitchcoin (2015)
why: Token backed by photographs, redeemable by burning; early supply/provenance work (check the provenance batch first).

name: Damien Hirst, other HENI NFT projects (2022–2023)
why: Check whether later HENI releases reused The Currency's choice-and-burn rule.

name: Kevin Abosch, Forever Rose / IAMA Coin (2018)
why: A 1/1 split among 10 co-owners and a 10-million-token self-portrait; ownership rules, not yet researched.

name: Alexis André, Friendship Bracelets (2022)
why: Generative bracelets meant to be gifted; possible circulation protocol.

name: Eve Sussman, 89 Seconds Atomized (Snark.art, 2018)
why: Video split into 2,500 tokens; owners can borrow atoms to reassemble the film — a co-ownership rule. Needs a primary source and image.

name: Jennifer & Kevin McCoy, Public Key/Private Key (Whitney, 2019)
why: Uses Monegraph to make 50 people museum donors of the work.

name: Scarab Experiment (2015)
why: Counterparty project that is both an artist collective and an artwork.

name: Coin Artist (Marguerite deCourcelle), Bitcoin puzzle paintings (2015–)
why: Paintings hiding bitcoin keys that crowds race to solve; collective solving is the work.

name: Memorychain (2017)
why: Community-driven Counterparty card initiative in Asia, similar to Rare Pepe, with daily/thematic rules.

name: Bitcorn (2018)
why: Counterparty simulation game: players harvest farms or publish corn meme cards over four years.

name: Pixel Map (2016) and WeiCards (2017)
why: Early Ethereum shared canvases with buy/rent rules, like the Million Ether Homepage; check authorship.

name: Conlan Rios, NFT-Scribe (2019)
why: Contract that lets ERC-721 owners append on-chain messages to their tokens.

name: Sarah Meyohas, Cloud of Petals (2017)
why: Sixteen workers archived 100,000 rose petals and each chose the most beautiful petal per rose; a labour protocol now backing Bitchcoin.

name: Moxie Marlinspike, First Derivative (2021)
why: dApp for creating and trading NFT derivatives that track an underlying NFT.

name: Rhea Myers, The Fractionalized Phallus (2025)
why: 30 glitched 3D-scan fragments sold as separate NFTs; fractional ownership as subject, check whether any rule links holders.

name: Rhea Myers, Ethereum Art Market (2014)
why: Early smart contract to register and sell digital artworks with optional royalties.

name: Simon de la Rouviere / Untitled Frontier, Logged Universe (2021–2023)
why: Story-linked on-chain drops where holding earlier NFTs grants free mints of later ones (Anchor Certificates, Paintings of Forgotten Souls, Little Martians, Daisychains).

name: Hundreds (attributed to Simon de la Rouviere in the brief)
why: No source found linking a work called Hundreds to him; verify authorship.

name: Sarah Friend, Perverse Affordances / Terraforming
why: Other works on isthisa.com; check for contract rules.

name: Marina Abramović, Rhythm 0 (1974)
why: Audience given 72 objects and a written instruction to use them on the artist; likely belongs to the social / performance batch.

name: Olafur Eliasson, The collectivity project (2005–)
why: City of white LEGO bricks built and rebuilt by visitors; check whether a written rule shapes behaviour.

name: Miranda July & Harrell Fletcher, Learning to Love You More (2002–2009)
why: Numbered assignments posted online, completed and uploaded by thousands; belongs to network/crowdsourced.

name: Lygia Pape, Divisor (1968)
why: Large white cloth with holes worn and moved by a crowd; belongs to social/collective-action.

name: Oulipo
why: Workshop of potential literature (1960–) inventing constraints for members and readers; decide whether a group-executed work passes.

name: Art by Telephone... Recalled (2012–)
why: Restaging by Sébastien Pluot and Fabien Vallos in which new artists and institutions realise the 1969 phoned instructions.

name: Allan Kaprow, Scales (1971) and Words (1962)
why: Further Kaprow activities/environments with visitor rules; Scales restaged at Tate Modern 2008.

name: Christian Marclay, Shuffle (2007)
why: Deck of 75 photo cards of musical notation found in the world, to be shuffled and performed by musicians; not verified this pass.

name: Christian Marclay: Festival (Whitney, 2010)
why: Graphic scores performed by about fifty musicians; visitors marked up a wall-size score.

name: Wolf Vostell, telephone happenings for Art by Telephone (1969)
why: Visitors dialled changing numbers to receive one-minute happening instructions.

name: Marcel Duchamp — Erratum Musical (1913)
why: Chance score: notes drawn from a hat, sung by Duchamp and his sisters; only three performers, check whether it passes the group test.

name: Marcel Duchamp — Monte Carlo Bond (1924)
why: Shares sold to fund a roulette system; belongs to social/economies.

name: Joseph Kosuth — One and Three Chairs (1965)
why: Certificate lets each owner re-make the photograph with a local chair; borderline execution work.

name: Lucy Lippard — 557,087 / 955,000 (1969–70)
why: Curator executed absent artists' instructions for the number shows.

name: Seth Siegelaub — The Xerox Book (1968)
why: Seven artists incl. LeWitt and Weiner given the same 25-page constraint; likely social/economies or theory batch.

name: Yoko Ono — Play It by Trust (1966)
why: All-white chess set that visitors play until they lose track of sides.

name: Yoko Ono — My Mummy Was Beautiful (2004)
why: Visitors leave written messages about their mothers (Tate Liverpool 2004, Tate Modern 2024).

name: Sol LeWitt — Wall Drawing #122 and other copy-line drawings
why: Drafters copy one another's not-straight lines; relatives of #797.

name: Jackson Mac Low: Three Social Projects (1963)
why: Chapter 7 of the Getty Scores Project; social instruction pieces by Mac Low, not yet researched.

name: Yvonne Rainer: We Shall Run (1963)
why: Dance score for untrained performers running in formation; Getty Scores Project chapter 8.

name: Takehisa Kosugi: Micro 1 (1961) / Theatre Music
why: Event scores in the Anthology and Fluxus; performed in 2021 for the Getty program.

name: Walter De Maria: Beach Crawl (1960)
why: Score in the Anthology of Chance Operations, re-performed as SKY, STONE, SEA (2021).

name: Earle Brown: December 1952
why: Graphic score that any instrumentation may interpret; strong visual; check whether group realizations make it pass.

name: Alison Knowles & James Tenney: The House of Dust (1967)
why: Computer-generated poem built as a structure at CalArts where students and artists staged works; borderline, the rule for the group is weak.

name: Nam June Paik: Zen for Head (1962)
why: Paik's realization of Young's Composition 1960 #10; could be a separate entry if Paik's scores for audiences (Participation TV) are covered.

name: Dick Higgins: Danger Music series
why: Fluxus event scores, some for audiences; not researched.

name: Flux Year Box 2 (c. 1966)
why: Second Fluxus anthology box with Fluxfilms and action kits; MoMA holds it; could join Fluxkit.

name: Fluxus 1 (1964)
why: First Fluxus yearbox anthology of scores by many artists.

name: Pauline Oliveros: Deep Listening practice / Deep Listening Institute
why: Ongoing practice with workshops and group pieces beyond Sonic Meditations.

name: John Cage: Variations VII (1966, 9 Evenings)
why: Live-electronic piece picking up sounds from phone lines and radio; Getty Research Institute video exists; check whether it passes (Cage and Tudor as performers).

name: Ulises Carrión, Erratic Art Mail International System (1977)
why: A postal art system with its own rules for sending and registering mail.

name: Image Bank (Vancouver), image request lists (1970–)
why: Artists posted lists of images they wanted; the network sent them in. Correspondence protocol.

name: Clemente Padín / Edgardo Antonio Vigo, Latin American mail-art networks
why: Mail art as political circulation under dictatorship.

name: Robert Filliou and Joachim Pfeufer, Poïpoïdrome (1963–)
why: Proposal for a 'permanent creation' centre; could not confirm a rule addressed to a group.

name: Superflex, Free Shop (2003)
why: Shops charge zero for an undisclosed period; staff follow the rule, customers react. Borderline.

name: Superflex, Corruption Contract (2009) and 2000 Watt Society Contract (2010)
why: Contracts imposed on clients or residents as artworks.

name: Carey Young, Declared Void (2005)
why: Visitors who enter a marked zone agree by contract to be under US constitutional jurisdiction.

name: Platoniq, Banco Común de Conocimientos (Bank of Common Knowledge)
why: Skill-exchange bank run as an artwork; sibling of Time/Bank.

name: Santiago Sierra, Persons Paid to Have Their Hair Dyed Blond (2001) and other paid-participant works
why: Same wage-contract protocol; add after checking media.

name: Cildo Meireles, Zero Cruzeiro / Zero Dollar (1974–78)
why: Artist-issued banknotes of zero value that entered circulation.

name: Temporary Services (Chicago)
why: Artist group producing free publications and exchange projects.

name: Joseph Beuys, Honigpumpe am Arbeitsplatz / Free International University (documenta 6, 1977)
why: 100 days of workshops run by different groups around a honey-pump circuit; check whether the workshop format counts as a group protocol.

name: Bill Wasik, The MOB Project (2003)
why: First flash mobs, organised by anonymous email instructions to a crowd; belongs to network/crowdsourced.

name: Yoko Ono, Cut Piece (1964)
why: Audience members cut the performer's clothes one by one; a close relative of Rhythm 0 (likely in the score batch).

name: Mieko Shiomi, Spatial Poem (1965–75)
why: Event instructions mailed to participants worldwide; responses mapped and published. Score or correspondence.

name: Suzanne Lacy, Whisper, the Waves, the Wind (1984) and Between the Door and the Street (2013)
why: Further large choreographed conversations with women; same protocol family as The Crystal Quilt.

name: Jeremy Deller, Procession (Manchester, 2009)
why: Parade made of groups who each chose how to represent themselves.

name: Tania Bruguera, Association of Arte Útil / Hannah Arendt International Institute for Artivism (INSTAR)
why: Institutions run as artworks; check rules and participation.

name: Marina Abramović, Abramović Method (2012–)
why: Instructions and exercises for audiences in groups; check if the group behaviour is the work.

name: Lee Mingwei, The Dining Project / Sonic Blossom / The Mending Project
why: Other gift-and-condition works where strangers carry out the protocol.

name: Hans Haacke, Gallery-Goers' Birthplace and Residence Profile (1969)
why: Visitors mark where they live on maps; audience produces the work's data.

name: Stephen Willats, West London Social Resource Project (1972)
why: Questionnaires and feedback loops with residents; systems-based participatory art.

name: Spencer Tunick, mass nude installations (1992–)
why: Thousands of volunteers follow posing instructions; borderline because the photograph is authored by one person.

name: Hélio Oiticica, Tropicália (1967) and Éden (1969)
why: Environments completed by visitors' behaviour; check whether a rule set exists.

name: Theaster Gates, Dorchester Projects / Rick Lowe, Project Row Houses
why: Social-practice institutions built with neighbourhoods; check whether the rules are authored and addressed to the group.

name: Marinella Senatore, The School of Narrative Dance
why: Nomadic school and parades produced by local participants under a method.

name: Jack Burnham, 'Real Time Systems' (Artforum, 1969)
why: Companion essay to Systems Esthetics on art as information and real-time process.

name: Roy Ascott, 'Behaviourist Art and the Cybernetic Vision' (Cybernetica, 1966–67)
why: Earlier Ascott text defining art as a behavioural system with feedback from participants.

name: Edward A. Shanken (ed.), Telematic Embrace (UC Press, 2003)
why: Collected Ascott writings (the 1990 essay is reprinted as chapter 16, DOI 10.1525/9780520935372-019).

name: Primavera De Filippi & Felix Beer, 'Protocol Art II' (Protocolized / Protocol Institute, 2025)
why: Lecture on protocol art as rule systems executed and modified by communities; check for Protocol Art I and a video.

name: Distributed Gallery / [aside] (Right Click Save interview 'The Aesthetic of a Protocol', 2024)
why: Collective that explicitly calls its practice protocol art (Ready-Made Token, Chaos Machine, time-locked NFTs); belongs to onchain batch.

name: Verse journal, 'Protocol Art, Museum Acquisitions, and Measuring Public Sentiment' (2024)
why: Interview by Mimi Nguyen and Malte Rauch with Distributed Gallery defining protocol art.

name: World Computer Sculpture Garden (curated by 0xfff, 2024)
why: A 'contract show' that exists only as an Ethereum contract (0x2a362fF002f7ce62D3468509dD2A4a9f5A8EBBb0); works by Rhea Myers, Sarah Friend and others. Onchain batch.

name: Outland, 'Breaking Protocol' (Ordinals art)
why: Essay treating the Ordinals protocol as an artist-made protocol maintained by collective inscription.

name: Kei Kreutler, 'Inventories, Not Identities' (2021)
why: First essay in the same Gnosis Guild series, on collective composable identity via multisigs.

name: Protocol Institute / Protocolized newsletter
why: Successor to Summer of Protocols; hosts lectures on protocol art and design.

name: Shannon Jackson, Social Works (Routledge, 2011); Pablo Helguera, Education for Socially Engaged Art (2011); Tom Finkelpearl, What We Made (2013)
why: Further participation-theory books not yet researched.

name: Max Haiven, Art after Money, Money after Art (Pluto, 2018); MoneyLab Reader (INC, 2015)
why: Texts on artist-made economies and currencies relevant to crypto-theory.
